title: Effects of sublethal, chronic heat exposure on reproductive organs in the simultaneous hermaphrodite Lymnaea stagnalis
content:
ABSTRACT
Although increasing temperatures are expected to affect reproductive processes, the impact of chronic sublethal warming on male and female functions remains poorly understood, particularly in simultaneous hermaphrodites. We investigated the effects of prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures with varying food availability on the development of the reproductive organs of the great pond snail (Lymnaea stagnalis), a simultaneous hermaphrodite. Juveniles were reared for 68 days at four temperatures (17.5, 20, 22.5 and 27.5 °C) under either limited or unlimited food regimes. At the end of the experiment, we quantified size and mass of the following organs: female accessory glands (albumen, muciparous and oothecal glands); the bursa copulatrix; and male organs (the prostate gland and the preputium). We also analysed shell shape using elliptic Fourier descriptors. Our analyses revealed that chronic warming reduced the dry weight and/or area of all reproductive organs, except the bursa copulatrix, after accounting for body size. Unlimited food consistently increased size and mass of the organs and partially offset the negative effects of temperature, such that the impact of temperature on some glands was only evident under limited food regimes. Shell shape analyses did not indicate a strong temperature-associated pattern, suggesting that the organ responses were not simply explained by major changes in shell outline. Our results demonstrate that sublethal chronic heat exposure can compromise the reproductive organs of both males and females in a hermaphroditic mollusc, but that high resource availability can mitigate these effects. These findings underline the importance of habitat conditions for population persistence in the context of climate warming.
